paragraphs: I want to ask whether, in the civil order, there can be any sure and legitimate rule for governing, if we take people as they are and laws as they could be. In this inquiry I will always try to join what right permits with what interest requires, so that justice and utility are never split apart.

I begin without arguing that my subject matters. People will ask whether I am a prince or a legislator, that I should write about politics. My answer is that I am neither, and that is exactly why I write about it. If I were a prince or a legislator, I would not spend my time saying what ought to be done. I would do it, or say nothing.

I was born a citizen of a free State and a member of the Sovereign. However little my voice may count in public affairs, the right to vote on them makes it my duty to study them. And whenever I think about governments, I am glad to find that my studies keep giving me new reasons to love the government of my own country.

Man is born free, and yet everywhere he is in chains. One man believes he is the master of others, yet he is more of a slave than they are. How did this change come about? I do not know. What can make it legitimate? I believe I can answer that question.

If I took into account only force and what follows from it, I would say: “As long as a people is compelled to obey, and does obey, it does well. As soon as it is able to shake off the yoke, and does so, it does better still. For it regains its liberty by the same right by which that liberty was taken away, so either it is justified in taking it back, or there was never any justification for those who took it.” But the social order is a sacred right, and it is the basis of all other rights. This right, however, does not come from nature, so it must be founded on conventions. Before I come to that, I have to prove what I have just asserted.
